abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Durum wheat (Triticum turgidum ssp. durum L.) is an important world food crop used to make pasta products. Compared to bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), fewer studies have been conducted to identify genetic loci governing yield‐component traits in durum wheat. A potential source of diversity for durum is its immediate progenitor, cultivated emmer (T. turgidum ssp. dicoccum). We evaluated two biparental populations of recombinant inbred lines (RILs) derived from crosses between the durum lines Ben and Rusty and the cultivated emmer wheat accessions PI 41025 and PI 193883, referred to as the Ben × PI 41025 (BP025) and Rusty × PI 193883 (RP883) RIL populations, respectively. Both populations were evaluated under field conditions in three seasons with an aim to identify quantitative trait loci (QTLs) associated with yield components and seed morphology that were expressed in multiple environments. A total of 44 and 34 multi‐environment QTLs were identified in the BP025 and RP883 populations, respectively. As expected, genetic loci known to govern domestication and development were associated with some of the QTLs, but novel QTLs derived from the cultivated emmer parents and associated with yield components including spikelet number, grain weight, and grain size were identified. These QTLs offer new target loci for durum wheat improvement, and toward that goal, we identified five RILs with increased grain weight and size compared to the durum parents. These materials along with the knowledge of stable QTLs and associated markers can help to expedite the development of superior durum varieties.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Wheat (Triticum ssp.) is one of the major global food crops, supplying approximately 20% of the calories in the average human's diet, and in 2020, it was grown on more land area than any other crop (FAOSTAT). Approximately 5% of total global wheat area is occupied by the tetraploid form of cultivated wheat known as durum (T. turgidum ssp. durum L., 2n = 4x = 28, AABB genomes), and approximately 40 million tons are produced per year (Arriagada et al., 2020). Durum has hard kernels and is used to make pasta, couscous, and other semolina products.

Grain yield is a quantitative trait controlled by a multitude of genes and pathways, many of which have complex interactions (Cao et al., 2020). Kernel weight, size, and shape, the number of kernels per spike (KPS), and the number of spikes per unit area all interact with one another to determine final grain yield (Brinton & Uauy, 2018; Cao et al., 2020; Gegas et al., 2010), with each component comprising various subcomponents, adding to the overall complexity of wheat yield. In addition, wheat is an allopolyploid, and the presence of multiple copies of yield‐associated genes on homoeologous chromosomes confounds the ability to determine the effects of individual loci (Borrill et al., 2018).

Although a few studies have been conducted to identify quantitative trait loci (QTLs) in durum wheat relating to yield component traits (for reviews, see Arriagada et al., 2020; Cao et al., 2020; Colasuonno et al., 2021), most of the work done to dissect the genetics of wheat yield has been conducted in hexaploid wheat (T. aestivum L., 2n = 6x = 42, AABBDD) (Cao et al., 2020). Cultivated emmer, T. turgidum ssp. dicoccum (Schrank) Schübl (2n = 4x = 28, AABB), is the progenitor of durum wheat. It was one of the first domesticated crops in the Fertile Crescent and instrumental in the rise of modern human civilization, but today it is grown only in isolated areas for local use (Zaharieva et al., 2010). Cultivated emmer arose due to mutations in the Br loci in wild emmer, T. turgidum ssp. dicoccoides (Körn.) Thell (2n = 4x = 28, AABB), which resulted in a nonbrittle rachis (reviewed in Faris, 2014). This trait prevented the spikelets from shattering and falling to the ground before physiological maturity, which allowed the early farmers to harvest the grain more easily. Although cultivated emmer lost the spikelet shattering trait, the seed was still non‐free threshing due to the q and Tg genes. Subsequent mutations at these loci led to the formation of today's fully domesticated free‐threshing durum wheat. As the immediate progenitor of durum wheat, cultivated emmer provides a rich source of genetic diversity and variation that may be exploited for durum variety improvement.

sec.p: To date, most QTL mapping studies in tetraploid wheat have been conducted using durum × durum or durum × wild emmer populations. Recombinant inbred line (RIL) populations with closely related parents often lack the power to detect QTLs due to the genetic similarities between the two parents. Durum × wild emmer crosses are highly polymorphic, but introgressing traits from wild emmer into the durum germplasm pool is often associated with deleterious linkage drag (Yu et al., 2019). Durum × cultivated emmer crosses generally have good levels of polymorphism and are useful for identifying beneficial alleles derived from both durum and cultivated emmer; cultivated emmer‐derived genes can be moved into elite durum germplasm with less deleterious linkage drag compared to wild emmer.

We recently evaluated a population of RILs derived from the North Dakota durum variety Divide and the cultivated emmer accession PI 272527 (referred to as Divide × PI 272527 [DP527] RIL population) (Peters Haugrud et al., 2023). In that work, 17 QTLs were expressed under both greenhouse conditions and multiple field seasons. PI 272527 contributed beneficial alleles for thousand kernel weight (TKW) and increased kernel area (KA), width, and length. Multiple RILs outperformed both parental lines for seed weight, including TKW, and seed size traits, illustrating that allelic combinations from durum and cultivated emmer parents can be beneficial for increasing durum yield.

Two durum × cultivated emmer RIL populations, one derived from crossing the durum cultivar Ben with the cultivated emmer accession PI 41025 (referred to as Ben × PI 41025 [BP025] RIL population) and the other derived from crossing the durum germplasm line Rusty with the cultivated emmer accession PI 193883 (referred to as Rusty × PI 193883 [RP883] RIL population), were evaluated in the greenhouse for various spike and domestication traits (Faris et al., 2014; Sharma, Running, et al., 2019). The BP025 population has also been evaluated for multiple agronomic traits, Fusarium head blight resistance, resistance to tan spot, and validation of the spikelet per spike gene WAPO‐A1 (Faris et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2020; Kuzay et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2014). The RP883 population has also been evaluated for resistance to tan spot (Liu et al., 2020) and stem rust resistance (Sharma, Zhang, et al., 2019).

In the previous studies, the BP025 population was evaluated in the greenhouse but kernel shape/size traits were not measured (Faris et al., 2014). Also, the RP883 population was evaluated in the greenhouse by Sharma, Running, et al. (2019), but the focus of the study was threshability and domestication, and kernel morphology was not evaluated. In this study, our two primary objectives were to (1) identify stable and common QTLs associated with yield components in the BP025 and RP883 populations expressed in multiple field environments; (2) determine which traits can be targeted for improvement by deployment of cultivated emmer alleles for associated QTLs; and (3) identify RILs with yield‐related characters significantly better than the durum parents. By using these two populations (BP025 and RP883), which each have an elite durum cultivar/germplasm line as a parent, we were able to test whether alleles from the cultivated emmer parental lines could be beneficial to potentially improve yield in elite durum cultivars. Together, the identification of stable and common yield QTLs and associated molecular markers, knowledge of which traits can potentially be improved through deployment of cultivated emmer alleles, and the identification of RILs containing desirable combinations of alleles that exhibit improved yield‐related characters should help to expedite the development of adapted durum varieties with enhanced yield and performance.

sec.title: Plant material
sec.p: Two durum × cultivated emmer RIL populations were evaluated for grain yield components under field conditions in North Dakota, USA. The BP025 population was developed by crossing Ben (PI 596557), a North Dakota hard amber durum variety (Elias &Miller, 1998), with PI 41025, a cultivated emmer accession collected near Samara, Russia. The BP025 population consists of 200 RILs developed by single‐seed descent and was advanced to the F7:8 generation. BP025 was genotyped using the 9k iSelect SNP array (Cavanagh et al., 2013), and the map was published by Faris et al. (2014). The RP883 population was developed by crossing the durum line Rusty (PI 639869) (Klindworth et al., 2006) with PI 193883, a cultivated emmer wheat accession collected near Shewa, Ethiopia. The RP883 population consists of 190 RILs developed by single‐seed descent and was advanced to the F7:8 generation. RP883 was genotyped using the 90k iSelect SNP array (Wang et al., 2014), and the map was published by Sharma, Running, et al. (2019). Both the 9k and 90k iSelect SNP arrays have been previously shown to provide adequate genome coverage for QTL mapping (Cavanagh et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014), with the BP025 linkage map having a density of 0.94 centimorgan [cM]/marker (Faris et al., 2014) and the RP883 linkage map having a density of 1.4 cM/loci (Sharma, Running, et al., 2019).

sec.title: Trait evaluation
sec.p: The two populations and parental lines were evaluated under field conditions for a total of three seasons each and were grown in a randomized complete block design with three replicates each season. Plants were grown in hill plots with each plot consisting of 10–15 seeds and considered an experimental unit. The BP025 population was planted and evaluated in 2017, 2018, and 2019. The RP883 population was evaluated in 2018, 2019, and 2020. The 2017, 2018, and 2019 plots were grown at the North Dakota State University field site near Prosper, ND (47.002°N, 97.115°W), and the 2020 plots were grown at the NDSU agronomy seed farm near Casselton, ND (46.880°N, 97.243°W).

The BP025 and RP883 populations and parental lines were evaluated for 11 traits including days to heading (DTH), plant height (PHT), the total number of spikelets per spike (SPS), KPS, grain weight per spike (GWS), TKW, KA, kernel width (KW), kernel length (KL), kernel circularity (KC), and kernel length:width ratio (KLW). The three main yield components of wheat are kernel weight/size, number of KPS, and spike number per unit area. Subcomponents for spike number per unit area were not evaluated in this experiment. TKW, KA, KW, KL, KC, and KLW are subcomponents of kernel weight/size. SPS and GWS are subcomponents related to the number of KPS. DTH and PHT are not components of yield but often highly correlated with final yield outcome. DTH was measured as the number of days from planting until 50% of the spikes emerged completely beyond the flag leaf. PHT was measured in centimeters from the base of the plot to the tip of the tallest spike (excluding awns). Eight heads were used for phenotypic evaluations. SPS was counted as the total number of SPS. KPS, GWS, TKW, KA, KW, KL, KC, and KLW were obtained using a MARVIN grain analyzer (GAT Sensorik GMBH). For KPS and GWS, the value obtained by the MARVIN for each sample was divided by the number of spikes in that sample to obtain KPS and GWS for data analysis.

sec.title: Statistical analysis and QTL mapping
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed using the PROC GLM procedure in SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute). Fisher's least significant difference (LSD) test was used to determine significant differences among the RILs with α = 0.05. For each population within each field season, Bartlett's chi‐squared test for homogeneity of error variances (Snedecor & Cochran, 1989) was used to determine if replicates within the same environment could be combined (Tables S1 and S2). For those traits that were not normally distributed, Levene's test (Levene, 1960) was used instead. For those that could be combined, the scores of each replicate for those traits were used to calculate the means, which were used for further analyses and QTL mapping. For RP883 traits TKW and KW evaluated in 2018 and PHT in 2020, replicates were not homogeneous using either Bartlett's or Levene's test. Therefore, each replicate for these traits was analyzed separately. Trait mean, maximum, minimum, and correlations were calculated in R v4.0.3, with Pearson correlation coefficients calculated using the R command cor (R Development Core Team) and plotted using R/corrplot (Wei & Simko, 2017).

QTL analysis was performed using R/qtl (Broman et al., 2003) using the same methods as described in Peters Haugrud et al. (2023). The final QTL model used was identified using multiple QTL mapping with a forward/backward search method and a maximum of 12 QTLs allowed (Manichaikul et al., 2009). QTL names include the trait abbreviation followed by “fcu,” the laboratory designation for J. Faris. LinkageMapView (Ouellette et al., 2018) in R was used to develop Figures S1 and S2.

Markers most significantly associated with each QTL were subjected to BLASTn searches against Svevo RefSeq Rel. 1.0 pseudomolecules (Maccaferri et al., 2019), Zavitan WEWSeq v2.0 pseudomolecules (Zhu et al., 2019), and the Chinese Spring IWGSC RefSeq v2.1 genome assembly (Zhu et al., 2021) using GrainGenes (Yao et al., 2022) to obtain the physical positions for comparing QTLs between environments and to identify known genes within each QTL region. The sequences for reported genes were obtained from GenBank or the published articles, which are cited in Supporting Information S1.

sec.title: BP025 trait evaluations
sec.p: For the BP025 population, we observed no significant differences in DTH, KPS, and KL between Ben and PI 41025 that were consistent across all three seasons; however, we did observe significant differences among the RILs, indicating that different genes were controlling these traits (Tables 1 and S3; Figures 1 and S3). Ben had increased GWS, TKW, KA, and KW compared to PI 41025, whereas PI 41025 had increased PHT, SPS, KC, and KLW. Significant differences were observed between the RILs for all 11 traits, indicating that transgressive segregation is occurring in this population.

sec.title: RP883 trait evaluations
sec.p: No significant differences that were consistent for all three field seasons were observed for traits SPS, GWS, TKW, KA, and KL between Rusty and PI 193883 (Tables 2 and S4; Figures 2 and S4). Rusty had increased DTH, PHT, KPS, and KW compared to PI 193883, and PI 193883 had increased KC and KLW. The ranges for RILs showed significant differences for all 11 traits indicating that, like the BP025 population, transgressive segregation occurred in RP883 as well.

sec.title: BP025 correlations
sec.p: Detailed correlation results for the BP025 population are presented in Tables S5–S7 and Figure 3. Some correlations were not consistent across environments. In two seasons, as the number of SPS increased, there was a significant increase in the number of KPS and GWS. KPS and GWS had a significant positive correlation in all three environments. The grain weight traits GWS and TKW had positive correlations with each other along with positive correlations with the grain dimension traits KA, KW, and KL, but they were negatively correlated with KC and KLW. The only yield component trait in which DTH had a consistent correlation was SPS, and it was a positive one. However, PHT had a negative correlation with KC and KLW. As for the grain dimension traits KA, KW, and KL, all had positive correlations with one another. KW was negatively correlated with KC and KLW, but interestingly, KL had a positive correlation with KC and KLW, which were also positively correlated with one another.

sec.title: RP883 correlations
sec.p: Detailed correlation results for the RP883 population are presented in Tables S8–S10 and Figure 4. As with the BP025 population, as SPS increased so did KPS, but there was no correlation with GWS. Additionally, SPS had a positive correlation with DTH. KPS and GWS were positively correlated with each other, but KPS had no correlation with TKW. GWS and TKW had positive correlations with each other and with PHT, KA, KW, and KL. TKW also had a negative correlation with KC and KLW. Interestingly, DTH was negatively correlated with KLW, but PHT had a positive correlation with KA, KW, and KL, even though DTH and PHT were positively correlated. The grain dimension traits KA, KW, and KL were all positively correlated, which was the same as the BP025 population. KA and KW were negatively correlated with KC and KLW, but as with the BP025 population, KL had a positive correlation with KC and KLW, which were also positively correlated with one another.

sec.title: QTL analysis in BP025
sec.p: Among the three environments for the BP025 population, we identified 164 significant QTLs and QTL × QTL interactions using forward/backward selection to identify the QTL model with the highest logarithm of the odds score. Within individual field seasons, 56, 59, and 49 QTLs were identified in 2017, 2018, and 2019, respectively (Table S11).

As previously mentioned, we were interested in identifying QTLs that were significant across multiple environments, that is, at least two of the three tested environments. Twenty‐six QTLs were observed in two environments, and 18 were observed in all three (Tables 3 and S11; Figures 5 and S1). If a QTL was identified in all three environments, we defined it as “stable,” and a stable QTL observed in both populations was defined as “common.” A total of 15 genomic regions were associated with the 44 QTLs that were observed in multiple environments. No QTL × QTL interactions were found to be consistent across environments.

sec.p: Many of the stable QTLs were associated with multiple traits (MT‐QTLs) and collocated with genetic loci for known genes such as ELF3, Ppd‐B1, Vrn‐A1, Q, and Vrn‐B1 (Tables 3 and S11; Figures 5 and S1). The ELF3 locus on chromosome 1A was associated with the kernel traits KL, KC, and KLW and explained 10.0%, 11.0%, and 9.9% of the variation in these traits, respectively. PI 41025 contributed to increased values for all three traits at the ELF3 locus. Ppd‐B1 on chromosome 2B was associated with DTH and SPS, explaining up to 6.6% and 13.1% of the variation, respectively. PI 41025 contributed to increased SPS, whereas Ben contributed to the desired value of a decrease in DTH at Ppd‐B1.

On chromosome 5A, Vrn‐A1 was associated with DTH and PHT, with PI 41025 contributing to a decrease in both traits (Tables 3 and S11; Figures 5 and S1). The Vrn‐A1 region explained up to 25.7% and 12.0% of the variation in DTH and PHT, respectively. Also, on chromosome 5A, the Q locus was associated with stable QTLs for SPS, KW, and KLW, explaining up to 14.6%, 7.9%, and 7.2% of the phenotypic variation, respectively. Ben contributed to an increase in SPS and KW at Q, whereas PI 41025 contributed to an increase in KLW.

The MT‐QTL associated with the most traits was Vrn‐B1 on chromosome 5B (Tables 3 and S11; Figures 5 and S1). QTLs for seven traits, SPS, TKW, DTH, PHT, KA, KW, and KC, co‐localized in this region. The Vrn‐B1 region explained the greatest phenotypic variation for DTH at 32.6%. Ben was the donor of the beneficial/desired alleles for SPS, TKW, KA, and KW at Vrn‐B1, whereas PI 41025 was at DTH, PHT, and KC.

Additional MT‐QTL regions were identified on chromosomes 1A, 2A, 3B, 4A, 5A, and 7A with no previously identified genes within 10 megabase (Mb) of the most significant single‐nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) (Tables 3 and S11; Figures 5 and S1). The MT‐QTL on chromosome 1A was associated with SPS, GWS, TKW, KA, and KW, explaining up to 7.1%, 8.8%, 9.7%, 10.7%, and 11.4% of the phenotypic variation, respectively, with Ben contributing the beneficial allele for all the traits. On chromosome 2A, a genetic region spanning 16.6 cM contained QTLs for KPS, TKW, PHT, KL, and KLW, explaining up to 12.4%, 9.0%, 23.2%, 15.5%, and 9.4% of the phenotypic variation, respectively. There were potentially two separate QTLs in this region because Ben alleles contributed to increased KPS and PHT, whereas PI 41025 alleles contributed to increased TKW, KL, and KLW.

Two MT‐QTL regions were identified on chromosome 3B (Tables 3 and S11; Figures 5 and S1). QTLs for GWS, TKW, KA, and KW co‐localized and explained up to 16.6%, 17.3%, 14.3%, and 10.0% of the phenotypic variation, respectively. Ben alleles contributed to increased grain weight and size in this region. The second MT‐QTL was associated with SPS and KL, explaining 11.2% and 12.8% of the variation, respectively. Ben alleles contributed to increased SPS at this locus, whereas PI 41025 alleles contributed to increased KL.

An MT‐QTL associated with TKW, KA, and KW was identified in a distal region of chromosome arm 4AS with Ben alleles contributing to increases in these traits (Tables 3 and S11; Figures 5 and S1). The QTLs for TKW, KA, and KW explained up to 7.1%, 7.4%, and 11.7% of the phenotypic variation, respectively.

An MT‐QTL on the short arm of chromosome 5A contained QTLs for SPS and PHT and explained 4.0% and 9.6% of the phenotypic variation, respectively (Tables 3 and S11; Figures 5 and S1). Increased SPS was due to PI 41025 alleles, whereas Ben contributed to the desired trait of shorter PHT.

Finally, an MT‐QTL on chromosome 7A was associated with KW, KC, and KLW (Tables 3 and S11; Figures 5 and S1). Ben alleles contributed to increased KW, whereas PI 41025 alleles contributed to increased KC and KLW. These QTLs explained 17.5%, 15.9%, and 12.5% of the variation in KW, KC, and KLW.

Only three non‐MT‐QTLs were identified in the BP025 population. Two QTLs on chromosome 3A for PHT and KL and a stable QTL associated with SPS on chromosome 7A were identified and explained 19.4%, 6.0%, and 17.9% of the variation, respectively (Tables 3 and S11; Figures 5 and S1). The QTL on chromosome 7A mapped to the known location of WAPO‐A1 with PI 41025 contributed to increased SPS at this locus.

sec.title: QTL analysis in RP883
sec.p: Among the three field seasons for the RP883 population, we identified 149 significant QTLs and QTL × QTL interactions (Table S12). Within individual environments, 64, 38, and 47 QTLs were identified in 2018, 2019, and 2020, respectively. A total of 17 QTLs were observed in two environments, and 17 QTLs were observed in all three environments (Tables 4 and S12; Figures 6 and S2). A total of 14 genomic regions were associated with these 34 QTLs, and no QTL × QTL interactions were consistent across environments.

sec.p: MT‐QTL regions for stable QTLs were identified in the RP883 population associated with loci harboring the known genes Vrn‐A1, Q, Vrn2, and FT‐1, which are located on chromosomes 5A, 5A, 5A, and 7B, respectively (Tables 4 and S12; Figures 6 and S2). Vrn‐A1 was associated with stable QTLs for TKW, DTH, KA, and KW and explained up to 10.6%, 27.7%, 10.6%, and 16.2% of the variation, respectively. Rusty alleles at Vrn‐A1 contributed to increased TKW, KA, and KW, whereas PI 193883 alleles at this locus contributed to the desired trait of decreased DTH.

Q was also associated with DTH and KW along with stable QTLs for SPS, KC, and KLW, and explained up to 16.3%, 9.5%, 15.2%, 11.2%, and 17.5% of the variation, respectively (Tables 4 and S12; Figures 6 and S2). Rusty alleles contributed to increased SPS, DTH, and KW, whereas PI 193883 alleles contributed to increased KC and KLW. Lastly on chromosome 5A, QTLs for TKW and DTH co‐localized near the Vrn2 locus and explained up to 8.7% and 7.6% of the variation in TKW and DTH, respectively, with PI 193883 alleles resulting in increased TKW and Rusty alleles in reduced DTH.

The FT‐1 region contained QTLs for DTH and PHT, with PI 193883 contributing alleles for decreased DTH and PHT (Tables 4 and S12; Figures 6 and S2). FT‐1 explained up to 17.2% and 6.6% of the variation in DTH and PHT, respectively.

Additional MT‐QTLs that are not associated with previously identified genes were identified on chromosomes 1B, 2B, 3A, 4A, and 6B. The MT‐QTL on 1B was associated with GWS, PHT, and KA, explaining up to 12.0%, 15.0%, and 13.3% of the phenotypic variation, respectively (Tables 4 and S12; Figures 6 and S2). Rusty alleles contributed to increased GWS and KA, whereas PI 193883 alleles contributed to the desired trait of reduced PHT. An MT‐QTL region on chromosome 2B was associated with four traits: KPS, KW, KC, and KLW. These QTLs explained up to 11.9%, 14.9%, 11.3%, and 9.8% of the variation in KPS, KW, KC, and KLW, respectively, and Rusty contributed to increased KPS, KC, and KLW, whereas PI 193883 contributed to increased KW.

On chromosome 3A, an MT‐QTL associated with TKW, KA, and KL was identified and explained up to 9.9%, 12.3%, and 16.2% of the phenotypic variation, respectively (Tables 4 and S12; Figures 6 and S2). PI 193883 contributed to an increase in value for all three traits. On chromosome 4A, another MT‐QTL was associated with TKW and KA, along with PHT. Rusty contributed to increased TKW and KA, whereas PI 193883 alleles resulted in the desired trait of shorter PHT. These QTLs explained up to 7.0%, 17.0%, and 6.9% of the variation in TKW, PHT, and KA, respectively. Lastly, an MT‐QTL on chromosome 6B was associated with SPS, KC, and KLW, explaining up to 15.9%, 15.3%, and 15.0% of the variation in these traits, respectively. Rusty alleles contributed to increased SPS, whereas PI 193883 alleles contributed to increased KC and KLW.

For non‐MT QTL, a stable QTL was identified on chromosome 1A for DTH, which mapped to the locus known to harbor the ELF3 gene (Tables 4 and S12; Figures 6 and S2). Additional individual stable QTLs on chromosomes 2A and 3A and two QTLs on chromosome 4B were associated with the traits KL, KL, DTH, and KW, respectively, and were not associated with loci known to harbor previously identified genes.

sec.title: Identification of RILs potentially useful for improvement of yield in durum wheat
sec.p: Analysis of the data from combining all the field environments revealed two BP025 RILs and three RP883 RILs that may be beneficial for improving grain weight and size in durum wheat (Figures 7 and 8; Tables 5 and 6). Two BP025 RILs, BP025‐38 and BP025‐146, had increased TKW values of 44.7 and 44.9 g, compared to Ben, but not increased KPS or GWS (Figure 7; Table 5). However, compared to Ben, BP025‐38 and BP025‐146 had increased KA, KL, and KC, with BP025‐146 also having increased KW. KA is the most desired seed trait for improvement, with this value being 19.3 and 19.8 mm2 for BP025‐38 and BP025‐146, respectively, compared to 18.5 mm2 for Ben. Neither BP025‐38 nor BP025‐146 had the desired allelic combinations for all the stable TKW or KA QTL.

sec.title: Known genes and durum‐derived QTLs
sec.p: The primary goal of this study was to identify cultivated emmer‐derived robust yield‐associated QTLs consistently expressed under field conditions that could potentially be used to improve durum wheat varieties. In pursuit of that goal, we identified QTLs associated with the known developmental genes WAPO‐A1, ELF3, Ppd‐B1, Vrn‐A1, Q, Vrn‐B1, Vrn2, and FT‐1. These genes have all been shown to influence various plant development, flowering, domestication, and yield component traits in wheat (Alvarez et al., 2016; Beales et al., 2007; Boden et al., 2015; Distelfeld et al., 2009; Dixon et al., 2018; Kippes et al., 2016; Nishida et al., 2013; Ochagavía et al., 2019; Royo et al., 2020; Simons et al., 2006; Würschum et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2003, 2006; Yan, Helguera, et al., 2004; Yan, Loukoianov, et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2020). ELF3 is a circadian clock regulator gene that is involved in controlling flower time and has been shown to be influenced by temperature (Alvarez et al., 2016; Ochagavía et al., 2019). ELF3 can influence Vrn2 and Ppd‐B1 as part of the wheat photoperiod regulatory pathway, which also interacts with Vrn‐A1, Vrn‐B1, and FT‐1 (Alvarez et al., 2023). Changes in any of these genes, due to expression, copy number variation, or allele present, can influence the number of DTH, resulting in changes in various yield component traits due to modification in the number of spikelets, grain number, and grain weight/size (Boden et al., 2015; Gauley et al., 2018; Glenn et al., 2022). The Q gene in wheat is an APETALA2 (AP2) transcription factor and is the major domestication gene in wheat, which results in naked grains and confers the free‐threshing character (Simons et al., 2006). An SNP in the microRNA172 binding site is responsible for the differences between q, which is non‐free‐threshing, and Q, which is the domestication allele (Debernardi et al., 2017). Q is part of a different pathway and has been shown to be involved in the expression of over 3000 genes and numerous pathways and may determine the final grain number in wheat through pollen fertility (Zhang et al., 2020). Durum wheat has Q, meaning it is free threshing, whereas cultivated emmer has q, which is non‐free threshing. Although all these gene regions coincided with multi‐trait, stable QTLs associated with yield component traits in the BP025 and RP883 populations, the desired alleles at these loci, with the exception of WAPO‐A1, are likely fixed in most durum breeding programs. Therefore, even though the data indicate that cultivated emmer alleles at some of these loci would be beneficial, they would simultaneously confer undesirable traits, which precludes them from being deployed for durum improvement.

For many of the stable QTLs that are not associated with known genes, the donor alleles for the desired traits such as decreased DTH and PHT, increased SPS, and increased grain number, size, and weight were contributed by the durum parents Ben and Rusty. As with beneficial alleles for known genes described above, the desirable alleles for many of these durum‐derived QTLs may already be fixed in many durum wheat breeding programs, but knowledge of their expression and stability makes them a priority for retainment when breeding programs are introducing diversity through wide crosses. The QTL‐associated markers identified in this research can be used in breeding programs for selection of the desirable alleles.

sec.title: Potentially useful QTLs derived from cultivated emmer
sec.p: QTL regions of interest in which the beneficial alleles were contributed by the cultivated emmer parent PI 41025 in the BP025 population included an MT‐QTL region on chromosome 2A, a QTL on chromosome 3A for KL, and QTLs on chromosomes 3B, 5A, and 7A for SPS. In the R8P883 population, QTL regions in which beneficial alleles were contributed by the cultivated emmer parent PI 193883 included an MT‐QTL on chromosome 3A, a QTL for DTH on chromosome 4B, QTLs for PHT on chromosomes 1B and 4A, a QTL for KW on chromosome 2B, and QTLs for KL on chromosomes 2A and 3A. Each of these QTLs are discussed in further detail below.

Within the BP025 population, a region spanning 16.6 cM and 85.2 Mb on chromosome 2A had QTLs associated with TKW, KPS, PHT, KL, and KLW. The gene GNI‐A1, which encodes an HD‐Zip I transcription factor, is located within this physical region based on the Svevo reference sequence (Sakuma et al., 2019). Sakuma et al. (2019) found that the level of GNI1 expression has decreased over the course of wheat domestication resulting in increased number of fertile florets per spike. Golan et al. (2019) reported the GNI‐A1 protein to be a transcriptional activator, and a reduction in kernel number resulted in enlarged and heavier kernels. In the BP025 population, increased KPS was conferred by Ben alleles, whereas increases in TKW, KL, and KLW were conferred by PI 41025 alleles. These findings are consistent with the relationship between grain number and grain weight governed by GNI‐A1 where a reduction in GNI‐A1 expression, which is common in domesticated wheat, results in an increase in the fertile number of florets per spike and increased number of KPS but smaller kernel weight/size (Golan et al., 2019; Sakuma et al., 2019). The PI 41025 allele of GNI‐A1 may be a strong candidate for introgression into durum germplasm for breeders interested in increasing grain size/weight; however, further field studies and validation are needed to determine the effects of these QTLs and their interactions with one another. Additionally, QTLs for KL and KLW were identified in this genomic region in the durum × cultivated emmer population DP527 (Peters Haugrud et al., 2023), with the emmer parent PI 272527 contributing to increased KL. The identification of this common QTLs between two populations indicates that this QTL would be an ideal candidate for breeders desiring to increase KL in their breeding programs, especially in North America; however, this may come at a cost of decreasing the number of kernels, and as stated above, additional work is needed to evaluate how breeding for the different alleles at this QTL affects overall yield.

Another MT‐QTL with desired alleles contributed by cultivated emmer was identified on chromosome 3A to be associated with TKW, KA, and KL in the RP883 population. In related work, we observed QTLs for TKW, PHT, KA, and KL near this physical region in another durum × cultivated emmer population, DP527 (Peters Haugrud et al., 2023). Sun et al. (2020) also observed QTLs within this region for TKW and kernel size, and Valladares García (2021) observed a QTL cluster for kernel size traits within this region in a durum × cultivated emmer population as well. Kernel size and weight are usually positively correlated; therefore, breeding for one often results in an increase in the other (Brinton & Uauy, 2018). The QTLs at this locus for TKW and KL were present in all three environments, indicating that these were stable QTLs in our experiment and would be good candidates to develop lines with the PI 193883 alleles within this region for germplasm improvement.

A stable and common QTL for KL was observed on the distal long arm of chromosome 3A in both the BP025 and RP883 populations, with the cultivated emmer parents in each population contributing to increased KL. As with the other common QTLs, the identification of QTLs observed across multiple populations with diverse cultivated emmer parents may be beneficial to breeding efforts for these traits.

In the BP025 population, three QTLs were identified in which PI 41025 contributed to increased SPS. Although there is often a trade‐off between increased SPS and grain size, if the desired outcome is to breed for increased SPS, we recommend introgressing the QTLs QSpn.fcu‐3B, QSpn.fcu‐5A.1, and QSpn.fcu‐7A. No known genes are associated with the two QTLs on chromosomes 3B and 5A. The QTLs identified on the long arm of chromosome 7A had the largest effect on SPS in the BP025 population. Previously, the 2017 and 2018 field data for the BP025 population were used to validate the candidate region for WAPO‐A1 (Kuzay et al., 2019). WAPO‐A1 encodes an F‐box protein and regulates floral organ identity (Kuzay et al., 2019, 2022; Muqaddasi et al., 2019; Voss‐Fels et al., 2019). Kuzay et al. (2019) found that in the BP025 population, PI 41025 contained the favorable haplotype for increased SPS. Further analysis of a diverse panel of diploid, tetraploid, and hexaploid wheat revealed that the WAPO‐A1b allele, present in PI 41025, is less frequent in modern cultivars than the other two WAPO‐A1 alleles. Almost all durum lines, including Ben, had the WAPO‐A1a allele, which confers a fewer number of SPS than the WAPO‐A1b allele. The results from our study, along with Kuzay et al. (2019), indicate that WAPO‐A1 can be used for increasing the number of SPS in durum wheat. We have already begun the backcrossing process to introgress the PI 41025 allele at WAPO‐A1 into a more suitable background for use in germplasm improvement.

Additional QTLs in the RP883 population were identified for DTH, PHT, KW, and KL in which the cultivated emmer parent PI 193883 contributed to the desired value. A QTL associated with decreased DTH was identified on chromosome 4B, whereas QTLs on chromosomes 1B and 4A were associated with decreased PHT. Further work is needed to unravel the effect of these loci along with the novelty and impact they could have in developing improved durum varieties. PI 193883 also contributed to an increase in KL and KW at QTLs on chromosomes 2A and 2B, respectively, and these QTLs may be useful for increasing diversity for these traits in durum breeding programs.

sec.title: Recommended RILs for durum breeding
sec.p: Two RILs from the BP025 population and three RILs from the RP883 population that had superior grain weight and size compared to both parents in their respective populations are recommended for incorporating desirable cultivated emmer‐derived traits into adapted durum lines to potentially increase overall yield. For our interest, we only looked at which QTLs each line had for TKW and KA due to these being the traits in which most breeding programs aim to increase; however, the data are freely available for others interested in QTLs for other traits. BP025‐38 can be used for introducing the QTkw.fcu‐2A from cultivated emmer into a breeding program, which is the only QTL for TKW and KA in which the alleles resulting in an increase are contributed by cultivated emmer. However, BP025‐38 and BP025‐146 can be used to incorporate QTLs derived from Ben for increased grain weight and size into a breeding program; furthermore, they are already free threshing and should cross easily into any program. One caveat while breeding with these two lines is that they both contain PI 41025 alleles in the Vrn‐B1 and Ppd‐B1 region. Unfortunately, neither of these RILs has the PI 40125 allele at WAPO‐A1, and therefore a different RIL would need to be selected to incorporate the WAPO‐A1b allele into a germplasm pool.

For the RP883 population, RILs RP883‐72, RP883‐114, and RP883‐145 had the desired allele from PI 193883 at the QTkw.fcu‐3A QTL, and all three had the desired alleles from Rusty at QTkw.fcu‐4A and QTkw.fcu‐5A.1. However, only RP883‐145 also had the desired Rusty allele at QTkw.fcu‐5A.2. To breed for increased TKW using these lines, a breeder would need to select for PI 193883 alleles at the 3A QTL but Rusty alleles at the other three QTLs. Unfortunately, although RP883‐72 had the highest TKW and KA, this line had PI 193883 alleles at Q, Vrn‐A1, and Vrn2. If a breeder desired to work with this line, an early objective would be to select against the cultivated emmer alleles at these loci. Both RP883‐114 and RP883‐145 had Rusty alleles at Q and Vrn‐A1, but RP883‐114 was the only one of the selected RILs with Rusty alleles at Vrn2. Based on our genetic analysis, if a breeder chooses to use one of these lines in a breeding program, we recommend RP883‐145 and eliminating the PI 193883 allele at Vrn2. The lines selected from both populations may prove beneficial to increasing grain weight and size in durum breeding programs; however, we have not tested if or how the beneficial cultivated emmer alleles might affect grain quality.

sec.title: CONCLUSIONS
sec.p: In this study, we identified multiple stable and common QTLs associated with various yield component traits in the BP025 and RP883 populations under field conditions. Although many of the beneficial QTLs were derived from the durum parents, the cultivated emmer parents contributed beneficial alleles for QTLs governing several yield components including the number of spikelets, grain weight, and grain size, thus demonstrating the potential for exploiting the genetic diversity existing in cultivated emmer for durum wheat improvement. Although many of our findings from durum wheat are similar to what was discovered in previous studies, we identified multiple novel QTLs for yield traits in which the beneficial donor was the cultivated emmer parent. These findings expand the repertoire of genes in tetraploid wheat that can be exploited for increasing durum wheat yield.

However, a few precautions should be considered when introgressing these traits from cultivated emmer. One caveat is there may be trade‐off between multiple yield component traits (e.g., increased SPS/KPS resulted in smaller kernels). Therefore, breeding for an increase in one trait may result in a decrease in another trait. In addition, linkage drag consisting of undesirable alleles including some of the major floral and developmental genes such as Q, Vrn‐A1, Vrn‐B1, ELF3, Ppd‐B1, and Vrn2 may pose some issues as well. If these lines are used in breeding programs, selection for the desired alleles at these loci in either the RIL used or in the breeding process will need to be a priority to develop free threshing lines with the desired developmental traits.

Although we studied yield component traits with the two populations, additional work is needed to evaluate quality traits and determine if either cultivated emmer accession possesses beneficial or detrimental QTLs governing quality traits. It would be beneficial to evaluate both the BP025 and RP388 populations for various quality parameters affecting durum wheat to determine if enhanced yield performance can be coupled with improved quality when exploiting allelic variation derived from cultivated emmer wheat. Additionally, the plot size used in this study was small (hill plots), and it is not a good indicator of what final yield would be for each line if a regular yield plot size and seeding rate were used. However, due to the population sizes and field constrictions, we decided to use hill plots, but if a breeder is interested in introgressing traits from the RILs, planting in larger sized plots is recommended. This would allow for a better estimate of overall plot yield versus just the various yield component traits we measured from eight heads per plot.

Screening panels of cultivated emmer accessions might be useful to identify additional emmer‐derived alleles for yield and other traits such as quality, disease/pest resistance, and environmental tolerance as well. In this way, the vast pool of cultivated emmer diversity can be further evaluated, characterized, and exploited for not only durum wheat improvement, but common wheat as well. Kuzay et al. (2019) sequenced the WAPO‐A1 locus in 70 cultivated emmer wheat lines and found only three to have the desired allele (WAPO‐A1b), with PI 41025 being one of them, demonstrating that beneficial alleles may not necessarily be abundant among cultivated emmer accessions and enhancing the need to survey a large number to identify useful genes and obtain accurate estimates of allele frequencies.

In summary, our results suggest that cultivated emmer can be a good source for improving yield component traits in durum wheat; however, as stated, other aspects such as quality still need to be evaluated. Additionally, markers associated with stable QTLs in these populations may be useful in breeding programs that implement genomic selection as fixed markers (Lozada et al., 2019; Sarinelli et al., 2019). Lastly, identifying yield component genes is critical for marker development, gene cloning, and unraveling the genetic mechanisms that determine final grain yield, which is necessary to increase overall yield and feed the world's growing population.

caption.p: Supplementary Figure 1. Linkage maps of chromosomes 1A, 2A, 2B, 3A, 3B, 4A, 5A, 5B, and 7A in the Ben × PI 41025 (BP025) recombinant inbred line population with the chromosomal locations of the 44 quantitative trait loci (QTLs) associated with the eleven traits evaluated under field conditions. Only those QTL which were identified in two or more environments are illustrated. Chromosomes 1B, 4B, 6A, 6B, and 7B are not shown because no stable QTL were detected on them in our study. The centimorgan scale (cM) is shown on the left of the figure, and along each chromosome on the right is the 9k iSelect SNP markers. QTL are shown along the right, with the peak marker ranges for the observed environments combined to encompass the QTL region. QTL with asterisks (*) around the name were observed under three field seasons whereas QTL without were observed under two field seasons. QTL with (RP883) behind the name were also observed in multiple field seasons in the Rusty × PI 193883 (RP883) recombinant inbred line population. QTL bars are color coded based on trait: dark violet (spikelets per spike), pink (kernels per spike), blue (grain weight per spike), coral (thousand kernel weight), dark green (days to heading), turquoise (plant height), brown (kernel area), light green (kernel width), tan (kernel length), plum (kernel circularity), maroon (kernel length:width ratio).
